title: The Queen of Madurai Who Died Behind a Locked Door | Mangammal #shorts

lines.text: A queen ruled Madurai for fifteen years. Nobody knows for sure how she died.
lines.caps: a *queen | ruled *Madurai | nobody knows | how she *died.

lines.text: Her name was Mangammal, of the Madurai Nayak kingdom.
lines.caps: her name was | *Mangammal | of the *Nayak kingdom.

lines.text: Around sixteen eighty nine, her son the king died young. Accounts say his widow died by sati, leaving a baby son.
lines.caps: around *1689 | her son | the king | died *young | his widow | died by *sati | leaving a *baby son.

lines.text: So Mangammal ruled as regent, for that baby, her grandson.
When a Mughal army pressed south, accounts say she chose to pay tribute, not fight.
lines.caps: a *Mughal army | pressed south | she paid | *tribute | not fight.

lines.text: But she also sent armies, against Travancore in sixteen ninety seven, and later against the Maratha ruler of Thanjavur.
lines.caps: she sent *armies | against *Travancore | in *1697 | and later | against *Thanjavur.

lines.text: She is remembered for roads. The old highway from Kanyakumari was once called Mangammal Salai.
lines.caps: she is remembered | for *roads | the old *highway | was called | *Mangammal Salai.

lines.text: And for rest houses, where pilgrims found shelter and food.
Her summer palace, Tamukkam, still stands in Madurai. Today it holds the Gandhi Memorial Museum.
lines.caps: her summer palace | *Tamukkam | still stands | today the *Gandhi | Memorial *Museum.

lines.text: Then the grandson came of age. Accounts say she would not hand over power.
lines.caps: then the grandson | came of *age | she would not | hand over *power.

lines.text: One later story says she was locked away, and slowly starved.
lines.caps: one later *story | she was | *locked away | slowly *starved.

lines.text: Food was placed outside, close enough to see and smell, but never to reach.
lines.caps: *food outside | close enough | to *see | and *smell | never to *reach.

lines.text: But a historian writing in nineteen seventeen called that source unreliable. The true cause, he said, may stay a mystery.
lines.caps: a historian | in *1917 | called it | *unreliable | the true cause | may stay | a *mystery.

lines.text: Her roads outlived her. Her last days left no clear record.
lines.caps: her *roads | outlived her | her last days | no clear *record.

sources.name: Mangammal (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: queen regent of the Madurai Nayak kingdom for her grandson Vijaya Ranga Chokkanatha; daughter-in-law committed sati; regency c. 1689-1704/05; tribute to the Mughals; expedition to Travancore (1697) and war with Shahaji of Thanjavur; roads (Mangammal Salai), choultries, Tamukkam summer palace; death c. 1705 surrounded by folklore of imprisonment and starvation

sources.name: R. Sathyanatha Aiyar, 'History of the Nayaks of Madura', The Indian Antiquary vol. 46 (1917), p. 197
sources.supports: the tradition (from a historian called 'most unreliable') that she was imprisoned and slowly starved with food placed where she could see and smell but not reach it; the author's conclusion that the true cause of her death is and is ever likely to be a mystery; a small room 'Mangammal's Hall' pointed out as the place of death

sources.name: Tamukkam Palace (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: summer palace of Rani Mangammal (c. 1670), now houses the Gandhi Memorial Museum, Madurai

sources.name: A Queen Who Would Not Yield (Swarajya)
sources.supports: Mangammal's regency, diplomacy with the Mughals, wars, public works

illustration: Mangammal, her son, her grandson and all soldiers and pilgrims are anonymous faceless figures; no portrait of any real person exists or is shown. Palaces, maps, roads and the locked room are stylised illustrations, not reconstructions. No inscription or quotation is shown.
uncertain: Dates differ by source: the regency is given as 1689 to 1704, 1705 or 1707; her death as about 1705.
The 'fifteen years' is approximate (1689 to about 1704).
The sati of her daughter-in-law and the details of the succession come from later accounts.
The imprisonment and starvation story is a later tradition; the 1917 historian who reported it called its source most unreliable. How she actually died is unknown.
Whether she was refusing to hand over power, or acting in good faith, is debated.
